idiom_name: sealed interface + data class / data object cases + exhaustive when
implementation_notes: Since Kotlin 1.5 the natural shape is a sealed interface (or sealed class) whose implementations are known at compile time, with one data class per legal variant and a when expression as the consumer - over a sealed subject the compiler demands that every case is covered and does not require an else branch. Implementations may live anywhere in the same package and module (the older nesting rule is lifted), which keeps the model and its consumers together; property-based data classes make the per-variant payload immutable and comparable. What replaces the classic closed class hierarchy is the sealed modifier plus exhaustiveness checking of when, which is a compile-time guarantee rather than a convention.
pitfalls: An else branch in a when over a sealed type disables the exhaustiveness diagnostic: the compiler accepts it and every future variant is silently absorbed by the else arm.

Direct subclasses must live in the same package and module; a variant declared elsewhere either does not compile or forces the sealed modifier off, and in multiplatform expect/actual code the common module still needs an else branch.

data class payloads are only shallowly immutable - a List or array component stays mutable, and the generated copy() lets callers change a field without validation, so keep fields private and expose factories that validate.

variants.name: Pre-1.5 sealed class with nested cases
variants.idiom_name: sealed class + nested data classes / objects + exhaustive when
variants.implementation_notes: On Kotlin 1.0-1.4 the realization is a sealed class whose variants had to be nested inside it (or in the same file), consumed by an exhaustive when - the same guarantee, one language floor lower and with the nesting restriction that keeps the whole model in one declaration. Choose this variant only for code that must keep compiling on an old Kotlin compiler; on 1.5 and later the sealed interface form is preferred because variants may be top-level in the same package and a class can implement several sealed interfaces.
pitfalls: Variants must be nested in the sealed class on this language floor - moving one out (a refactor that is legal on 1.5) stops the file compiling on 1.4 and earlier.
The same else-branch trap applies: an else arm compiles and silently disables exhaustiveness for future variants.
Sealed classes cannot be implemented from another module, so a consumer that needs to extend the set must be part of the same compilation unit - do not promise extensibility you cannot deliver.
